title.title: Every admissible base is a primitive root infinitely often
title.subtitle: Claim: if $a \ne -1$ is not a square, at least $c_a x/(\log x)^2$ primes in $(x, 2x)$ have $a$ as primitive root

object.caption: odd primes $p$; marked: the powers of $2$ run through every nonzero residue mod $p$

beats.text: Is $a$ a primitive root mod $p$, so that its powers hit every nonzero residue?
Artin (1927): yes for infinitely many $p$, unless $a = -1$ or $a$ is a square
Claimed: infinitely many for every admissible $a$, though not Artin's predicted density

sources.quote: For every integer a that is not -1 and not a perfect square, at least c_a x/(log x)^2 primes in (x, 2x) have a as a primitive root, for all large x
Artin (1927). Hooley (1967) proved the full density conjecture under GRH for Kummer fields.
at most two prime bases fail, so one of 2, 3, 5 works, but no specific base was known.
Proves infinitude with x/(log x)^2, not Artin's predicted density A(a) x/log x, so Artin's conjecture in its quantitative form remains open.
The analytic input (Theorem 1.2) is itself an enormous claim

plain: Powers of a number like 2 cycle through every remainder mod $p$ for infinitely many primes $p$, as Artin guessed

steps: Show certain $L$-functions have no zeros in a wide strip
Sieve for primes $p$ where $p - 1$ factors in a controlled way
Together they give many primes where $a$ is a primitive root

data.result: infinitely many primes, for every admissible $a$

voice.text: Do the powers of a hit every nonzero remainder mod p, for infinitely many primes?
A zero-free region plus a sieve on p minus one give many primes.
